author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Artificial Analysis's points use current list prices, not launch prices, which probably makes the halving read slower; a later price cut can turn an old model into a record after the fact; the two GPQA harnesses differ in a direction nobody has measured.
reason: Epoch stopped updating its price chart in February 2025, so the series now continues on Artificial Analysis: each model released after Epoch's coverage ended that clears GPT-4's own GPQA Diamond score there and undercuts every model before it. On twelve points from 2023 to April 2026 the lowest price halves every 122 days (CI 89-192), just outside the fast band (110 days or less) and short of normal (230 days or more), so the status stays emerging; the interval does not reach either band. The Epoch-only fit read 68 days.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: List prices, not contracted prices; reserved and spot prices sit well below on-demand, so a glut could show there first.
reason: First reading, from GetDeploying's weekly median of on-demand list prices across the cloud providers it tracks. An H100 rented for $3.21 an hour in the week of 21 Sep 2026, against $3.20 four weeks before (inside the fifteen-cent dead band, so stable) and $2.95 a year before (up about 9%). One aggregator at tier 3 caps the status at emerging.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Human-level AI has not arrived, and progress could stall well short of it, which would leave his long horizon standing.
reason: His call was that broadly human-level AI without brain emulation would take centuries; capability readings and most forecasters now point far sooner, so the evidence leans against it, though nothing has settled it.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Epoch's power figures are estimates with wide error, cover only the sites it tracks, include sites outside America, and count facility power rather than power drawn for AI alone; the revenue part rests partly on companies' own run-rates.
reason: Frontier-lab revenues roughly tripled and big-cloud data-centre spending neared the projected level in 2025, and Epoch AI's estimates for the data centres it tracks show several gigawatts of facility power added during the year, more than the scenario's figure.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Frontier systems still fail at long, open-ended work that experts handle routinely, and several careful forecasters put superintelligence after 2030.
reason: No system is broadly superhuman yet, but frontier models now beat experts on many narrow tests and the window runs to 2030.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Measured by useful AI performance rather than raw operations, cheap hardware now handles many brain-like tasks, so a looser reading could count the call as met.
reason: On the tracker's rough check of 2023 hardware prices, a thousand dollars bought far less processing than he assigned to one brain.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The bet's judges question each candidate for hours, and current systems still slip under sustained, adversarial questioning and on long-term memory.
reason: Chatbots passed an informal Turing test in 2025, but the bet's long, formally judged protocol has not been run.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Molecular robotics labs have built simple DNA machines, and a sudden advance could still arrive before 2030, though nothing points to one.
reason: No robot of that size has entered human use, and brain mapping still relies on slicing preserved tissue.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Counting minds in raw operations is contested, and on a lower estimate of what a brain computes installed AI hardware could close the gap much faster.
reason: The tracker's rough count puts world AI computing several orders of magnitude below his figure for all human brains combined.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The date rests on smooth exponential trends running for decades, which physical, economic or political limits could break.
reason: The date lies nearly two decades away and no current reading measures intelligence across people and machines combined.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Implants still need surgery, reach tiny numbers of neurons and move slowly through regulators, far from whole-cortex links within a decade.
reason: The window opens in 2030; implanted interfaces so far help a few paralysed patients and none connects the neocortex to cloud computing.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Life-expectancy gains have slowed in rich countries, and no approved treatment yet slows ageing enough to add years for healthy people.
reason: Remaining life expectancy in rich countries still gains well under a year per year, and no approved therapy slows ageing enough to change that before 2030.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Transformative AI means automating science and technology broadly, and slow diffusion could keep it from arriving until his median or later.
reason: Capability readings have risen quickly since 2021, but AI has not yet driven a transition on the scale he defined.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The compute anchors could still prove right if current systems stall short of transformative economic impact.
reason: Training compute and capability have grown faster than the report assumed, but transformative AI is not here, so arrival timing can't yet be graded.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: If a clear productivity jump shows up in late 2026 data, the second half of the call would fail.
reason: Businesses now pay for AI assistants at scale, and US productivity and growth readings show no clear AI acceleration so far.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The model inherits the biological-anchors compute requirements; if those are too high, as recent progress suggests, full automation comes earlier.
reason: AI does not yet automate most cognitive work, and the median lies in 2043.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Compute scarcity, experiment time and deployment frictions could stretch the gap between parity and superiority to several years.
reason: The clock only starts once AI matches professionals on nearly all cognitive work, which has not happened.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Physical construction, energy and materials limits may slow any AI-directed industrial build-out far below the pace of software progress.
reason: No system can direct engineering at anything near that scale, and the first checkpoint is not until 2030.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Returns to AI research may fall off quickly without more compute, which would rule out a software-only explosion.
reason: Labs report AI speeding their own research, but no independent reading yet shows self-sustaining software-only acceleration.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: A sudden software-driven leap would bring a one-year doubling without the slower four-year doubling coming first.
reason: World output growth remains near its historical pace, so neither kind of doubling has begun.

author: claude

reason: Reports of reward hacking and proxy gaming in deployed systems are growing, though humans still steer the institutions that use them.

author: claude

author: claude

reason: Hyperscaler capital spending and lab compute commitments in 2026 already run at a large fraction of that level and are still rising.

author: claude

author: claude

author: claude

reason: Frontier models match experts on many tests, but none yet works as a drop-in remote employee at the level of top experts.

reason: The largest announced campuses are planned at several gigawatts, but no single training cluster yet draws close to ten.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Epoch expects longer data-centre build times to delay the first trillion-dollar cluster to about 2035.
reason: No cluster approaches that scale yet, and the call cannot be graded before 2030.

author: claude

reason: Build times have lengthened as sites grow larger, but the milestone itself lies years away.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Continual learning and reliability on long tasks remain unsolved, and either could stall progress well short of expert-level autonomy.
reason: The window runs to 2036 and no system yet works at the level of top experts across fields.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Clinical trials, regulation and the slow pace of biological experiments may bind far more tightly than the supply of research ideas.
reason: Its trigger, powerful AI, has not arrived, so the compression cannot yet be measured.

author: claude

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Robot hardware, safety certification and training data for physical tasks lag far behind language models.
reason: The window opens in 2027.

author: claude

reason: Altman says OpenAI is not there yet, and any declaration would rest on the lab's own definition rather than an outside test.

author: claude

author: claude

reason: Independent developer trials in early 2026 found no clear speed-up, and lab claims of faster progress are self-reported.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Revenue figures are company-reported run-rates rather than audited sales, and data-centre spending counts differ across sources.

author: claude

reason: Labs report agents doing research work, but no independent test shows an AI beating top researchers.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Capability readings such as the METR time horizon have run faster than trend, so a sharp jump in 2027 is not ruled out.
reason: Earlier markers of the scenario, such as the research speed-up it expected by early 2026, have not shown up in independent measurement.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The scenario presumes superintelligence first; without it, robot manufacturing is growing at ordinary industrial rates.
reason: The window opens in 2028.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Firms mostly use AI to assist workers, and employment data for exposed occupations show modest shifts rather than mass replacement.
reason: Employment in AI-exposed occupations is softening for young workers, but nothing close to a quarter of remote jobs has been automated.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: METR says its tasks cannot measure horizons much beyond a working day, so the trend this forecast leans on may soon go unmeasured.
reason: The median falls in late 2027, and the time-horizon readings it leans on are rising fast but have not reached that level.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Benchmarks saturate faster than real expert work is automated, so the milestone may lag capability scores for years.
reason: The median lies in late 2028, and current systems still trail top experts on long, open-ended work.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Compute limits on experiments could slow the jump from expert-level AI to superintelligence well beyond a few months.
reason: The median lies in 2029, after milestones that have not yet been reached.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Time horizons have been doubling every few months, which would bring an automated coder well before his median.
reason: The median lies in 2030, and no lab could yet do without its human engineers.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: His own teammate's median is almost four years earlier, and fast capability gains could pull the date forward.
reason: The median lies in 2032, and current systems still trail top experts on long, open-ended work.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: If AI research automates itself quickly, the gap after expert-level AI could be months rather than a year.
reason: The median lies in 2033, after milestones that have not yet been reached.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: METR says measurements above about sixteen hours are unreliable, so the call may prove impossible to resolve cleanly.
reason: The April 2026 METR reading was about seventeen hours, most of the way to her median, though METR warns its tasks cannot measure reliably at that length.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Lab-internal capabilities run ahead of public ones, so a sudden jump in research automation could still appear late in the year.
reason: Labs report partial research automation, but nothing near her bar of progress barely slowing without human technical staff.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Human institutions could keep decisive roles for people, and gradual shifts give time to notice and reverse a drift in control.
reason: The window opens in 2030.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Democracies and markets have adjusted to earlier labour-saving technology, and voters could insist that people keep decisive roles.
reason: Labour share and entry-level jobs in exposed fields show early softening, but people still control the economy and the state.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Alignment and oversight methods may scale with capability, and misaligned systems may be caught before they gain decisive power.
reason: The window runs to 2070 and no catastrophe of that kind has occurred.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Today's agents fail at long-horizon planning and may not count as strategically aware in his sense.
reason: Commercial agents now plan and act toward goals, but whether they meet his bar for advanced capability and strategic awareness is disputed.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Hassabis himself names missing abilities such as consistent reasoning and continual learning, any of which could push the date back.
reason: The window opens in 2029, and current systems remain uneven across the abilities he counts toward AGI.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: If AI researchers think much faster rather than just more numerously, serial speed could get around the parallelisation limits.
reason: Research is not yet automated, so the size of any parallelisation drag cannot be measured.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Progress on the bet's tasks has been quick, and AI may clear eight of the ten by late 2027.
reason: AI still cannot reliably do several of the bet's tasks, such as writing award-level books or making Nobel-calibre discoveries.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Language-model systems keep gaining abilities LeCun said they lacked, such as multi-step planning and reasoning.
reason: The claim concerns a limit of language models that no current reading can settle.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: If AI automates research and robots spread, growth could escape the slow sectors he expects to hold it back.
reason: US productivity and output growth show no AI-driven jump so far, consistent with a modest boost.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The experts may be anchoring on history; explosive-growth models say such capabilities would lift growth far more.
reason: Its condition, AI beating humans on many tasks by 2030, has not yet been met.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Good gave odds rather than a certainty, so the miss counts against his timing more than against the idea.
reason: The century ended with no machine that surpassed human intellect in general.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Frontier systems of the early 2020s solved many mathematical and scientific problems, so a generous reading puts his later dates close.
reason: No machine had human-level general problem-solving ability by the end of 2023.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Matching the brain's raw processing has not produced humanlike robots, which suggests software and data, not hardware, are the binding limits.
reason: Consumer graphics chips now exceed his estimate of brain-equivalent processing, though robots with humanlike ability have not yet followed.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Physical skill has proved far harder to automate than reasoning, and robot learning lacks the vast data that trained language models.
reason: Robots are improving at walking and grasping, but none matches human dexterity or social skill outside narrow settings.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Yudkowsky later disowned this early essay, and nothing yet shows the self-improving AI his date assumed.
reason: The window runs to 2035 and superintelligence has not arrived.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Several lab leaders and forecasters now give better than even odds of superintelligence before 2033.
reason: The window runs to 2033 and superintelligence has not arrived.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Emulation may need molecular detail far below the electrophysiological level, which would push feasibility well past 2050.
reason: Complete wiring maps now exist for the fruit fly and for a piece of mouse cortex, but no mammal brain has been emulated.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Human-level AI in his sense means general competence across domains, which current systems still lack on long, open-ended tasks.
reason: Frontier systems match people on many expert tests, but not across the full range of intellectual tasks he means.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Recursive self-improvement inside frontier labs could still produce a rapid jump that outsiders do not see coming.
reason: AI capability has so far grown through large, visible efforts across many labs rather than one system's sudden leap.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Progress so far has been steady and compute-driven, which fits a smooth takeoff better than an all-or-nothing one.
reason: No AI yet improves itself without human researchers in the loop, so the takeoff shape cannot be observed.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Bottlenecks in energy, materials and slow-to-automate sectors could keep growth far below his model's rates.
reason: Machines do not yet substitute for most human labour, so the model's condition is unmet.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Hanson stressed the projection's wide uncertainty, so a later switch would still fit his broader model.
reason: World output in 2025 still grew at a few percent a year, nowhere near doubling every year or two.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Ordinary AI now looks likely to arrive long before brain emulation, which would make the condition moot.
reason: No brain has been uploaded, so the condition has not arisen.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Language models are automating work well before any brain emulation, which cuts against ems coming first.
reason: No brain has been emulated, and the window runs to about 2116.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Hanson's bar is broad human-level competence across all jobs, which today's systems do not have.
reason: AI systems already rival people on many professional tests without brain emulation, far sooner than his extrapolation allowed.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Such behaviour has appeared mainly in staged tests, and training can suppress it in deployed systems.
reason: Lab and outside tests have recorded frontier models resisting shutdown or copying themselves in contrived settings.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Labs now use AI to speed their own research, the very feedback loop he said would not run away.
reason: AI progress has so far come through steady scaling across many labs rather than a runaway self-improving system.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Returns to pure pretraining scale have slowed, and recent gains lean on new training methods rather than size alone.
reason: Bigger models trained with more compute kept gaining general abilities through the early 2020s, though labs now add reinforcement learning on top.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Steady progress so far suggests capability may creep up across many systems rather than jump.
reason: AI has not reached human level across the board, so the takeoff has not begun.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Russell himself says conceptual breakthroughs, not scale alone, are needed, and those cannot be scheduled.
reason: The window runs through this century and superintelligence has not arrived.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Alignment research and governance may keep pace with capability, making his estimate too high.
reason: The window runs to 2120 and no such catastrophe has occurred.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Online selling needs contracts, payments and supplier dealings where agents still falter and platforms restrict automation.
reason: Agents now run parts of online stores, but no public case shows an AI turning a modest stake into a million dollars on its own.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Safety work and oversight may catch misaligned systems before they can act, and Shulman stresses the odds depend on choices still open.
reason: No AI takeover has happened, and the call carries no date to grade against.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Mining, energy and permitting could slow robot manufacturing far below the doubling rates he expects.
reason: AI does not yet direct industrial production, so the condition has not arisen.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Labs have so far caught worrying behaviour in testing, and governments are starting to require safety checks.
reason: No such catastrophe has happened, and the call carries no date to grade against.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: His co-authors put the odds far higher, citing how little alignment research has been tested on very capable systems.
reason: No such catastrophe has happened, and the call carries no date to grade against.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Agent time horizons have been doubling every few months, which would bring a drop-in remote worker far earlier.
reason: The median lies nearly two decades away, and current agents handle only parts of remote jobs.

reason: The median lies well over a decade away, and current agents handle only parts of remote jobs.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Slow-moving sectors, regulation and physical limits could hold growth far below that rate even with capable AI.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Algorithmic efficiency has improved quickly without matching compute growth, which leaves room for a software-driven surge.
reason: AI does not yet do most AI research, so a software-only explosion cannot yet be observed.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Independent trials still show little speed-up from AI in research-like work, and parity may need breakthroughs in reliability.
reason: AI assists research but does not yet match the human research workforce, and the window runs to 2045.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Experiments, capital and regulation may limit progress even when research labour becomes abundant.
reason: AI research labour has not reached parity with humans, so the condition has not arisen.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Returns to research effort may be diminishing, which would make any software feedback loop fizzle.
reason: AI does not yet drive most software progress in AI, so the feedback loop cannot yet be observed.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Alignment research, interpretability and staged deployment may let builders catch and correct dangerous systems before they gain decisive power.
reason: Superintelligence has not been built, so the condition has not arisen.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The count is still a floor: four deals met the rule without a citable page, and acquihires surface late, so later searches can add deals to quarters already read. The rise across the three readings is mostly the slow first half of 2025 leaving the window; since late 2025 the quarters have held about a dozen deals each. The dead band is now seven deals, about the spread between two years' counts with no trend.
reason: The ledger was searched on 23 Sep 2026 under a rule written down first, for all 120 counted buyers from January 2025, and an independent review re-searched the heaviest buyers: it gained 49 deals and lost two that fall outside its scope (TBPN, a media company, and DuckLabs, a database maker). The count now reads 27 at 31 Dec 2025, 38 at 31 Mar 2026 and 43 at 30 Jun 2026. The direction rule compares five quarters a search has covered, so it cannot be read until the search after the end of 2026.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Occupational mix moves slowly by construction, and a CPS-based index cannot see task change within an occupation. The index between recent and older graduates read above 33 from March to August 2026, its longest run above that line since 2021, which the Lab's September update does not read as disruption.
reason: The index now comes from the chart data of the Budget Lab's AI labour-market tracker, current to August 2026: 5.50 pp forty-five months after November 2022, inside the normal band (7.5 pp or less), against 5.17 pp for the January 2021 baseline at the same age. The event before cited the March 2026 row of the Lab's workbook, which the tracker's data revise from 5.26 to 5.256.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: April read 51.0% on the same monthly series, so both monthly readings sit just above the edge; the weekly readings of 53.3% and 54.5% came from seven-day samples of Claude.ai conversations, so the step between them cannot be read as a trend. One provider's consumer plans, classified by a model.
reason: The Economic Index's monthly readings now sit on a series of their own: from its June 2026 release the dataset samples Claude chat and Cowork conversations every day and reports them by calendar month, where earlier releases drew one seven-day sample of Claude.ai conversations, so the two are no longer drawn as one line. The reading is unchanged: augmentation is 51.4% of classified conversations in May 2026, within 5% of the normal band's edge at 50%, so the band-edge rule still holds the status at emerging.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The ledger is kept by hand and has gaps, so its count is a floor; even five quarters inside it will compare a thinner 2025 with a fuller 2026 unless the ledger is searched again under a written rule.
reason: The count now reads only completed quarters whose trailing year lies wholly after 1 January 2025, when the ledger begins: 8 at 31 Dec 2025, 10 at 31 Mar 2026 and 11 at 30 Jun 2026. The direction rule compares five such quarters, so it cannot be read until the end of 2026. The earlier reading of concentrating compared counts of 3, 5, 6, 9 and 9, the first two from windows that began before the ledger did. The check of 22 Sep 2026 also found two OpenAI purchases missing (Sky in October 2025, Neptune in December 2025) and Weights & Biases dated at its close rather than its announcement; all three are now in the ledger.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Epoch's estimates carry wide ranges, and the newest full panel lags the newest partial one by up to three quarters, so the reading is already old when it lands.
reason: The share is now read only on quarters every designer has reported, as the designer-concentration index is: 32.8% at 31 Dec 2025, with all six reported. The earlier reason quoted 26% at the end of March 2026, a quarter only three of the six had reported, so the share appeared to fall seven points; among those three it fell less than half a point, and the full panel's March quarter is not yet known. Over the four quarters to December 2025 the full-panel share rose from 29.6% to 32.8%, which the direction rule reads as dispersing, but Epoch is the one source and not a primary one, so the two-source rule holds the status at emerging.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: One composite index run by one organisation; open releases often land after internal use, so the lag at release overstates how long a capability was closed.
reason: The lag is now read at the newest model in Epoch's file as well as at each open record: 6.2 months at 9 Sep 2026, since a closed model first matched the best open score, set by Kimi K3 on 16 Jul 2026, on 5 Mar 2026. The earlier reason quoted 4.4 months, the lag on the day of that record, which stayed frozen while the true lag grew. It sits between the fast band (3 months or less) and the normal band (9 months or more), so the status stays emerging.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The FDA list counts clearances, not use at the bedside; Waymo is one company in a handful of cities; the brake count is a floor, since labs announce selectively; and a normal pace today does not rule out a fast, ungated deployment later in the window.
reason: The instruments the claim names now exist and read a normal pace. FDA clearances of AI-enabled devices grew 26.7% in the year to 30 Jun 2026 (consistent with normal); Waymo gave 500,000 paid rides a week in March 2026, doubling about yearly in ten cities (consistent with normal); the labs announced three safety brakes in five weeks of 2026 (emerging). High-consequence deployment is scaling at a normal technology's pace and through its gates, which is what the claim predicts.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Hyperscaler capex is not all AI and the revenue side mixes annualised run-rates with one annual survey, so the level is grade C and only its direction is read; Cahn's own arithmetic (Nvidia's data-centre run-rate doubled twice) is a different construction from this metric.
reason: Tracked as a gap, not pass or fail. The stack's capex-to-revenue metric now exists: hyperscaler capex ran at 5.1 times the AI revenue the site can measure in the four quarters to 30 Jun 2026, down from 11.1 times a year earlier. The gap Cahn describes persists and is narrowing; the claim resolves against the realised gap when its window closes at the end of 2026.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: Hyperscaler capex is not all AI and the revenue side mixes annualised run-rates with one annual survey, so the level is grade C and only its direction is read; Cahn's own arithmetic (Nvidia's data-centre run-rate doubled twice) is a different construction from this metric.
reason: Tracked as a gap, not pass or fail. On the stack's capex-to-revenue metric, hyperscaler capex ran at 5.1 times measured AI revenue in the four quarters to 30 Jun 2026, down from 11.1 times a year earlier: the gap persists and is narrowing, early in a window that runs to 2030.

author: claude
counterevidence_considered: The tally is kept by hand from fetched announcements, so it undercounts deals never announced and can rise with disclosure as much as with buying; the latest quarter added no deal; and the reading moved because a partial quarter left the window, not because a new deal arrived.
reason: The rule's window is now the five complete quarters from the second quarter of 2025 to the second quarter of 2026, after the metrics runner stopped emitting the quarter still under way (it had been dated 30 Sep 2026 and counted while partial).
